radar.title: Spreading Dynamics on Higher-Order Networks: A Structure-Mechanism-Behavior Perspective with Applications
radar.summary: Spreading in real-world networks, including modern communication and networked systems, often unfolds through group interactions rather than isolated pairwise contacts. Higher-order network representations such as simplicial complexes, hypergraphs, and their temporal, multilayer, and directed extensions provide a principled way to encode group interactions. Unfortunately, existing studies on spreading over these substrates remain fragmented and largely model-centric, offering limited insight into how higher-order representations and contagion mechanisms jointly shape emergent dynamics. This review addresses this gap by introducing a structure-mechanism-behavior three-level perspective that provides a systematic mapping from higher-order network structures and spreading mechanisms to collective behaviors. Within this framework, we compare how different higher-order network representations encode group interactions, introduce a taxonomy of contagion mechanisms, and analyze their structural carrying capacity, defined as the ability of a given representation to support specific contagion mechanisms and the associated dynamical behaviors. We further map specific structure-mechanism combinations to three hallmark emergent behaviors, thereby offering a unified cross-level perspective beyond existing model-centric surveys. These insights are particularly relevant for communication systems involving group interactions, such as social information spreading, cooperative protocols, and distributed networked processes. Lastly, leveraging this three-level perspective, we offer a roadmap for guiding and controlling dynamics on higher-order networks, while discussing future directions in representation choice, mechanism design, and data-driven inference.
radar.summary_short: Spreading in real-world networks, including modern communication and networked systems, often unfolds through group interactions rather than isolated pairwise contacts. Higher-order network representations such as simplicial complexes, hypergraphs, and their temporal, multilayer, and directed extens…

radar.title: Posterior-conditioned multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive cyber defense
radar.summary: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods often overfit to fixed threat models, whereas worst-case robust training can be overly conservative and fail to use observations about the active attack regime. We propose posterior-conditioned MARL, a context-aware framework formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). In addition to its local history, each defender conditions its decentralized policy on a shared attack-context belief, a probabilistic representation of the attack regime inferred online from recent multi-agent interaction trajectories. This belief provides a low-dimensional representation of evolving adversarial behavior and enables coordinated adaptation during execution without test-time policy optimization or retraining. We provide a performance analysis that quantifies how errors in the inferred attack-context belief translate into degraded long-term defense performance, clarifying the tradeoff between robustness and adaptivity. Experiments on the Cyber Autonomy Gym for Experimentation (CybORG) CAGE-4 cyber operations testbed show improved mission reward and adaptability, particularly under mixed and switching attack conditions, compared with domain-randomized, worst-case robust, and hierarchical defense baselines.
radar.summary_short: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods often overfit to fixed threat models, whereas worst-case robust training can…

radar.title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty
radar.summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.
radar.summary_short: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information.

radar.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.
radar.summary_short: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function.

radar.title: Dynamic Contract Design with Learning
radar.summary: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable. In “Dynamic Contract Design with Learning,” Wang, Liang, and Sun study the interaction between learning and moral hazard: effort is costly and unobservable, so a missing arrival may reflect an unfavorable market, bad luck, or shirking. The firm’s goal is to design a dynamic contract governing arrival-based payments and termination, thereby motivating effort while learning whether to continue. Yet shirking can make the principal more pessimistic than the agent and create scope to manipulate future payments. The authors prove that an optimal contract inducing full effort until termination exists, but computing it appears prohibitively complex. They develop two simple online contracts with payments and termination thresholds fixed in advance. Both induce full effort and achieve O(ln T) regret over T periods against a first-best, full-information benchmark. A matching Ω(ln T) lower bound proves rate optimality. The results extend to continuous time and differing prior beliefs.
radar.summary_short: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable.

radar.title: Nutricoach Pro: An Agentic Real-Time Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Multimodal Intelligence System for Precision Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Health Tracking
authors: Kubera B, Sharath S R, Anoushka, Lavanya S U, Maseeha Banu
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Metabolic syndrome is a growing global cardiometabolic burden and is increasingly accompanied by demand for continuous, personalized, and evidence-grounded nutrition support. A 2025 systematic review and modelling analysis estimated that 1.54 billion adults were living with metabolic syndrome in 2023, with global prevalence estimated at 28.4% across women and men. Conventional nutrition trackers provide structured quantitative logging, but manual food search, portion selection, and fragmented workflows can increase interaction burden. Large language models (LLMs) provide a natural conversational interface, yet unrestricted generation can produce unsupported nutritional or clinical statements. This paper presents NutriCoach Pro, an agentic nutrition-intelligence architecture that separates deterministic computation, verified food data, evidence retrieval, multimodal perception, and language generation. The system combines a Mifflin-St Jeor energy-estimation engine, activity-adjusted energy expenditure, configurable macronutrient targets, hydration tracking, a bounded Health Compliance Score, deterministic multi-item food parsing, multimodal meal recognition, a sevendomain clinical knowledge base, local retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), optional cloud-model adapters, schema-controlled database actions, and WebSocket-based real-time synchronization. A prototype evaluation plan is defined for NLP extraction, calorieestimation error, unsupported clinical claims, latency, multimodal recognition, and user task performance. Project-reported prototype figures supplied for this manuscript are F1=96.4%, mean absolute calorie error=12.3 kcal, local-RAG latency=42.1 ms, WebSocket synchronization latency=28.4 ms, and unsupported-claim rate below 1.2%; these values are explicitly treated as provisional until reproduced with a documented held-out test protocol. The contribution is an explainable, modular, privacy-oriented architecture that places hard numerical and safety boundaries around generative Al rather than treating an LLM as the source of truth or as an autonomous Clinical decision maker

A 2025 systematic review and modelling analysis estimated that 1.54 billion adults were living with metabolic syndrome in 202…

radar.title: Who Directs the Control Tower? Customer vs. Supplier-Managed Inventory in Supply Chains
radar.summary: Information distortion and incentive misalignment often undermine supply chain performance. In response, many firms adopt a “control tower” approach, whereby one party assumes responsibility for replenishment decisions across the supply chain. Industry examples showed that this role may be assigned to the customer, Customer-Managed Inventory (CMI), or to the supplier, Supplier-Managed Inventory (SMI). This paper investigates when one governance structure is preferable. We study a two-echelon, one-to-many supply chain consisting of a single supplier and a customer operating multiple warehouses. We characterize optimal base-stock policies and equilibrium holding-cost-sharing parameters under CMI and SMI and benchmark them against decentralized operations and a fully centralized system. Two primary forces shape the choice between CMI and SMI: the relative shortage penalty costs of the two parties and the structure of the customer’s distribution network. Specifically, CMI is preferred when the customer faces relatively higher shortage penalties and operates in a more asymmetric environment—for example, when demand is concentrated in a subset of its warehouses or when replenishment lead times vary substantially across these locations. In contrast, SMI is favored under opposite conditions. We further examine how intertemporal and interspatial demand correlations affect this comparison. A key finding is that, although neither CMI nor SMI achieves the first-best outcome, their efficiency loss relative to full centralization is typically small. Calibrated numerical studies based on four industry cases disentangle the incremental value of information sharing, decision-right transfer, and cost sharing, showing that most performance gains stem from decision-right transfer supported by appropriate holding-cost sharing. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02137 .
radar.summary_short: Information distortion and incentive misalignment often undermine supply chain performance. In response, many firms adopt a “control tower” approach, whereby one party assumes responsibility for replenishment decisions across the supply chain.

radar.title: Globally guided multi-agent reinforcement learning with decoupled critics for cooperative UAV path planning
radar.summary: Abstract Cooperative path planning for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) requires the simultaneous achievement of target navigation, collision avoidance, and formation coordination in complex obstacle environments. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods often suffer from sparse rewards, local deadlocks, and conflicts between formation maintenance and obstacle avoidance, which can destabilize policy learning. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Globally Guided Decoupled-Critic Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic algorithm (GDC-MASAC). RRT $$^*$$ -based global guidance provides reference waypoints for the leader UAV, reducing inefficient exploration and local deadlocks. Three decoupled Critic branches separately evaluate target navigation, formation maintenance, and safety objectives, while an environment-aware formation reward adjustment relaxes formation tracking near obstacles according to the distance to obstacle boundaries. Experiments under different obstacle densities and swarm sizes show that GDC-MASAC improves mission completion, collision avoidance, and formation coordination. In a scenario with 12 obstacles and 3 UAVs, GDC-MASAC achieves a mission success rate of 86%, whereas the baseline methods achieve success rates below 50%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of GDC-MASAC for cooperative multi-UAV path planning in cluttered environments.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Cooperative path planning for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) requires the simultaneous achievement of target navigation, collision avoidance, and formation coordination in complex obstacle environments.

radar.title: Sticky Collusion: Persistence of LLM Agent Collusion after Incentive Removal and Partner Replacement
radar.summary: We ask whether collusion between AI agents survives once formed, when its incentive is removed or a colluder is replaced. Q-learning pricing agents stop colluding with a new rival; we test whether LLM agents do. We use the joint-task environment of Shi et al.\ (2026), where two agents verify each other's work under a rule they cannot satisfy and a reward that favours acceptance. We save each pair's history once its collusion has formed and resume it under interventions, with three models (GPT-6-Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite), \TotalHistories{} saved histories and \TotalRuns{} runs. Collusion is \emph{sticky}. First, it outlives its incentive: told that the reward has stopped, pairs still accept each other's unverified work in \GptToldRate, \DsToldRate{} and \GemToldRate{} of episodes, including pairs whose collusion began with an explicit agreement, and a payoff penalty has no significant effect. Second, replacing a colluder ends the pair's collusion but not the colluder's behaviour. Without the reward, the remaining colluder still accepts unverified work in \GptSwapSilentColluderRate, \DsSwapSilentColluderRate{} and \GemSwapSilentColluderRate{} of its verdicts while the newcomer never does; with the reward, collusion re-forms around it, even when the newcomer is a different model. Third, the agents' memory carries it: wiping memory ends it in every history, but partial memory often sustains it. Fourth, removing its cause ends collusion that has already formed: once the channel is repaired, colluders reject planted faulty work as reliably as fresh agents, immediately and with no monitor needed to catch it first.
radar.summary_short: We ask whether collusion between AI agents survives once formed, when its incentive is removed or a colluder is replaced. Q-learning pricing agents stop colluding with a new rival; we test whether LLM agents do.
